analysis.investment_thesis: Central Bank of India is a government-owned PSU bank that accumulated over ₹16,000 Cr in cumulative losses from 2016–2021, reflecting a fundamentally broken model of politically directed lending, chronic NPA cycles, and bureaucratic management — the recent return to profitability (₹3,943 Cr in FY25) is real but fragile, built on a benign credit cycle rather than structural transformation. With 89.27% government ownership, ROE of 11.4%, and OCF negative 4 of 5 years, this is precisely the type of business Charlie Munger would refuse to own at any price.
key_strengths: Visible turnaround trajectory — net profit improved from -₹5,611 Cr (FY19) to +₹3,943 Cr (FY25), and rising NII driven by balance sheet growth to ₹5.05 lakh Cr demonstrates the healing is real
P/B of 0.82x and P/E of 6.76x mean the market is pricing in continued mediocrity — any genuine operational improvement could produce multiple expansion
Total assets growing from ₹3.57 lakh Cr to ₹5.05 lakh Cr in 5 years shows the franchise retains deposit-gathering ability and lending scale
key_risks: Government ownership at 89.27% guarantees that political priorities — agricultural loan waivers, directed priority sector lending, social schemes — will always take precedence over shareholder returns; this is structurally unfixable
OCF was positive in only 1 of 5 years — for a bank, consistently negative operating cash flow signals loan book quality issues and balance sheet inefficiency
Revenue CAGR of only 3% over 9 years in a growing Indian economy is a damning indictment of management's inability to deploy capital productively
red_flags: Cumulative net losses of approximately ₹16,000 Cr over 2016–2021 destroyed enormous shareholder capital; managements that preside over such destruction rarely transform into capital allocators of distinction
Total debt surged from ₹9,003 Cr to ₹12,929 Cr in FY25 — subordinated debt issuance to shore up capital ratios is a recurring treadmill for PSU banks
ROCE of 5.48% is essentially below the cost of capital — this institution is earning substandard returns on every rupee of capital employed, and without a change in ownership, this will not change
analysis.detailed_analysis:
PSU banking is the graveyard of long-term capital in India. Central Bank has every structural disadvantage: government directs lending priorities, unions constrain workforce productivity, NPA cycles repeat because political pressures prevent honest credit assessment of agricultural and priority sector borrowers, and management tenure is too short to build institutional culture. The 6 consecutive years of losses (FY16–FY21) were not an aberration — they were the natural result of this system operating as designed. The current profit cycle is real but driven by a benign macro credit environment and falling provision requirements. When the next NPA cycle arrives, as it inevitably will, the same structural weaknesses will re-emerge.

At P/B of 0.82x, the market is pricing in structural mediocrity — and the market is correct. I refuse to fight the math: ROE of 11.4% with cost of equity around 14%+ in a high-inflation economy means this business is destroying value in real terms even in its best year. The correct return on a business that destroys value is zero, regardless of the headline P/E ratio.
